extracted.intended_audience: students and authors in mathematics and computer science (papers, theses, books, literate programs, user manuals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing, presenting, and typesetting mathematics and computer-science technical documents (papers, proofs, algorithms, programs, theses, manuals) with emphasis on clarity, notation, organization, and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate symbols in different formulas with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols in different formulas must be separated by words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: "Consider S_q, q < p." Good: "Consider S_q, where q < p." Always place words between adjacent formula fragments so the reader can parse the relation between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't start a sentence with a symbol; begin with words instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "x^n - a has n distinct zeroes." Good: "The polynomial x^n - a has n distinct zeroes." This improves readability and sentence rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical shorthand symbols in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use symbols like ∴, ∀, ∃, ⇒ (except in logic works); replace them with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the corresponding words in normal mathematical exposition so prose reads smoothly for general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-into theorem statements with a complete sentence or colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement just preceding a theorem, algorithm, etc., should be a complete sentence or should end with a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fragments like "We now have" followed by "Theorem." Instead write a motivating complete sentence such as "We can now prove the following result:" or tie motivation to prior discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make theorem statements self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of a theorem should usually be self-contained, not depending on assumptions in the preceding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restate necessary assumptions inside the theorem to avoid forcing the reader to track back to previous paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' to avoid passive voice carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'we' is often useful to avoid passive voice and to create an author-reader dialog; avoid 'I' in most technical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' in contexts where it truly means 'you and me together'; for multiple authors, clarify if necessary (e.g., 'one of the authors (DEK)'). Consider alternatives (imperative/indicative) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sentence rhythm and readability; include 'that' when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences have a rhythm; read aloud and change wording that doesn't flow. Don't omit 'that' when it helps parse the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words/phrases for cadence; keep reader expectations in mind. E.g., include 'that' after 'assume' or 'suppose' when needed to help parsing, but avoid unnecessary padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow 'assume'/'suppose' with 'that' normally
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'assume' and 'suppose' should usually be followed by 'that' unless another 'that' appears nearby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't write awkward constructions like 'We have that x = ...' — write 'We have x = ...'. Use 'that' to aid clarity when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure; avoid echoing unusual words; use parallelism
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary sentence structure and word choice to avoid monotony; use parallelism where concepts are parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating unusual or 'sticky' words in consecutive sentences. Favor parallel constructions when comparing or listing analogous items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid homework-style formula listing; use running commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write a sequence of formulas merely listed; tie concepts together with running commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain transitions, motivations, and how displayed formulas relate; provide signposts and narration to guide the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: State definitions/important items twice in complementary ways
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to state things twice in complementary ways (e.g., formal definition and an informal description) to reinforce understanding; define all variables when first introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both an intuitive description and a formal definition for difficult concepts; ensure variables are at least informally defined at first occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always motivate what follows; keep reader's knowledge in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivate the reader for what follows: what they know so far, what they should expect next, and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing others' work, either let results speak or give reasons why they're interesting; when describing your own work, be humble and avoid superlatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure sentences still flow if formulas are skimmed
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers skim formulas on first reading, so sentences should still flow smoothly when formulas are mentally replaced by placeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write prose that links and explains formulas succinctly; avoid overdependence on long inline formula chains for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent notation; don't reuse symbols for different things
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use the same notation for two different things; conversely, use consistent notation for the same thing across the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow typographic conventions (lowercase for set elements, uppercase for sets) where appropriate; choose index ranges sensibly and stick to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts and avoid subscripted subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get carried away by subscripts; avoid subscripted subscripts by using set-element notation or naming elements only when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible refer to unspecified elements of a set rather than naming every element; reduce clutter and indexing complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important formulas; number only important ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Display important formulas on their own line; number the important ones only (not every displayed formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a formula will be referred to from remote parts of the text, give it a number; avoid numbering every displayed equation as it distracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sentences readable left-to-right; avoid ambiguous constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should be readable left to right without ambiguity; avoid constructions that force backtracking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast ambiguous phrases (e.g., "In the theory of rings, groups and other algebraic structures are treated") into unambiguous wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out small numbers used as adjectives; use numerals when numbers are names
rubrics_metrics.description: Small numbers should be spelled out when used as adjectives but not when used as names (i.e., when talking about numbers themselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., write "Method 2 is illustrated" but "it requires seventeen passes" when wording as adjective vs counting usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize theorem/lemma/algorithm names in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names like Theorem 1, Lemma 2, Algorithm 3, Method 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such named items as proper labels in headings or captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch common style maxims but apply them sensibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of preposition placement, dangling participles, sentence fragments, pronoun agreement, unnecessary commas, and split infinitives — but apply rules sensibly rather than slavishly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some 'rules' (e.g., never split infinitives) can be broken for emphasis; prefer clarity and cadence over rigid adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'that' vs 'which' appropriately; 'fewer' vs 'less'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'that' when it sounds better (restrictive clause) and reserve 'which' for nonrestrictive clauses; use 'fewer' for countable items and 'less' for uncountable quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the clause is essential to identify the noun, use 'that' (no commas); otherwise 'which' with comma may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening paragraph and first sentence should be best
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening paragraph should be your best paragraph and its first sentence your best sentence; a bad start can turn readers off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bland generic openings like 'An x is y.' Use motivating, contextual openings that hook the reader and suggest why the topic matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow conventional punctuation with quotation marks but be logical for strings
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal rule places commas and periods inside quotation marks; other punctuation stays outside unless part of the quotation. When quoting exact symbol strings, use strictly logical punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., Good: Always end your program with the word "end". For parentheses and brackets, maintain logical punctuation (period inside parentheses iff the whole sentence is inside).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long noun-strings as adjectives and unnecessary jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist long strings of nouns used as adjectives; avoid jargon when a non-specialist term would suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite awkward noun strings (e.g., 'packet switched data communication network protocol problem') and prefer clear vocabulary readable by a broader audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with humor and exclamation points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use humor only when readers who know the technical point will also appreciate the joke; avoid excessive exclamation points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor should not distract from the technical idea; exclamation points can be used sparingly or parenthesized for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas; avoid dangling operators or symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Always place words between adjacent formulas or symbols to clarify relationships and avoid ambiguous phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: 'Add k times to c.' Better: 'Add k copies of p to c.' Ensure formulas are embedded in grammatical sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ellipses and spacing carefully in formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: When using ellipses (PI, ... , Pn), put commas before and after the three dots; set the vertical level of dots appropriately (midline when bracketed by operators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch spacing around ellipses so character strings like '. . . ;' don't look odd; TeX spacing helps but authors must inspect output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid line breaks in the middle of formulas; control breaks with typesetting tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Linebreaks in the middle of formulas are undesirable; use typesetting controls (e.g., TeX) to prevent bad breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nonbreakable spaces or explicit commands (e.g., tilde in TeX) to keep related symbols together; avoid final symbol being isolated on its own line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be stingy with typographic tools and fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overuse typographic devices (many fonts, excessive boldface, all-caps); they distract and suggest shouting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic emphasis judiciously and consistently; rely on good structure rather than decorative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize nested parentheses and avoid bracket misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid nested parentheses when possible; don't replace outer parentheses with brackets/curly braces unless semantically appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nested groupings are necessary, ensure typography (larger outer delimiters) makes structure clear; avoid creative delimiter use that confuses readers in scientific contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering formulas: number only the ones you will refer to
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbering all displayed formulas is usually a bad idea; number only the important ones that will be referenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraneous equation numbers clutter the text; pick and number key equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before use and reduce unnecessary notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define symbols before you use them (or very near their use); reduce the number of distinct symbols if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing multiple similar notations that force the reader to remember many meanings; prefer clear, minimal notation that suits the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear signposting, transitions, and conversational tone for organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide signposts, transition paragraphs, and a conversational tone to guide the reader through proofs and long arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide proofs into parts, say 'first prove X then Y,' and use small remarks like 'the operative word is zero' to keep the reader oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary proof by contradiction; prefer direct proofs when available
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction are often less readable; use direct proofs when they exist and make exposition clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While contradiction is useful when discovering a result, present the clearest direct argument in the final exposition if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use boxes or Q.E.D. convention to mark proof end; format carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Paul Halmos' convention: place a box at the end of a proof (or Q.E.D.); leave a space between the final period and the box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The box serves as a clear visual end-of-proof marker; ensure punctuation around it is typographically correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in wording to avoid misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words precisely (e.g., 'not nonincreasing' vs 'increasing') and avoid sloppiness that changes mathematical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term has specific technical meaning (nonincreasing vs increasing), use the correct phrase and, if necessary, define terms explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent tense strategy (present or sequential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either use present tense throughout or write sequentially (mix tenses to indicate timing), and be consistent in your choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential writing uses phrases like 'We saw this before. We will see this later.' Present-tense uniformity may be simpler for shorter papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt organizational focus: 'Do organize' and 'Do not distract'
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material so the exposition has structure beyond linear order; avoid distractions that don't help communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave branches and threads together; avoid notation changes or stylistic shifts that distract unless used intentionally to jar the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional copy-editing and iterative rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in rewriting, proofreading, and (where feasible) professional copy editors or designers to improve typography and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should rewrite multiple times (example rewrite sequence shown by Knuth); designers can set margins, fonts, and make the text readable. Use spelling checkers and external reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with hyphenation and domain-specific compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide hyphenation for domain-specific compounds (e.g., 'programming-language notation' vs 'programming language notation') based on audience conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In computer science, many compounds are conventional without hyphens; follow discipline norms to avoid awkward hyphenation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation conventions for parenthetical material must be logical
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation inside parentheses should be correct independently of outside context; put a period inside parentheses only if the enclosed text is a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the parenthesized statement would be removed, both the inner and outer punctuation should still be correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coincident-punctuation paranoia; follow standard rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincident commas or punctuation marks (comma+period) are not problematic — follow the ordinary typography rules (write only one mark where coincident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., where a comma would coincide with a period, write the period; don't overreact to coincident punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tilde or nonbreaking spaces to prevent undesirable line breaks (TeX tip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nonbreaking space constructs (e.g., tilde in TeX) to tie words/symbols so they don't break across lines awkwardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leaving the final symbol alone on a line; use typesetting features to control linebreaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch spacing and typesetting of special symbols (empty set, mid) in TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of TeX commands for correct symbol spacing and representation (e.g., \mid, \emptyset) when writing mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrectly typed symbol sequences or spacing around ellipses and delimiters create ugly output; inspect compiled output carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with pronoun/gender choices and avoid needless clutter
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose pronouns in a way that serves clarity and audience expectations; avoid awkward 'he or she' repetition if it distracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate exists (use 'he', 'they', or other constructions); prefer forms that minimize distraction and maintain readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words like 'then' judiciously in mathematical contexts for parsing
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, leaving in 'then' after a conditional comma can aid parsing; decide based on context and reader speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For natural-language sentences outside math, 'then' is often omitted, but in technical/mathematical commas it may help comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive colons; capitalize after colon only when a full sentence follows
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overdo colons; capitalize the first word after a colon only if the following phrase is a full sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use colons for full-sentence introductions but omit when a displayed formula merely completes the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with coincident commas and commas-in-series
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincident commas are not inherently bad; write one punctuation mark when two would coincide and follow logical punctuation rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't avoid grammatically correct commas because they appear near other punctuation; clarity and grammar govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose tone/style appropriate to audience and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable tone varies across genres (journal articles, textbooks, manuals); choose a formality level and style (use of 'we', humor, imperative) appropriate to the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course accepts many genres (sonnets-programs, user manuals, journal articles). Pick conventions appropriate to the specific audience and document purpose.
